channel.title: AI Brief for Coaches & Small Business
channel.description: What's changing in AI that actually affects coaches and small businesses, in plain language. New issues every Tuesday and Friday by 7 a.m. Eastern.

item.title: Friday, October 2, 2026: OpenAI teams up with small business centers on AI training, and publishes a report on small-team use
item.description: This week's useful news is mostly about the everyday basics of using AI at work. Research suggests the way leaders talk about AI shapes whether their people actually use it. Security and privacy keep coming up, from small-business cyber threats to a patched flaw in a popular chat app. The tools you may already use, like Google Workspace and Shopify, keep shifting under you, and a new wave of personal AI agents is arriving. Most of this week's other AI headlines were about big-company deals and models, and none of them changed much for a solo practice or small team.
item.content:encoded:
This week's useful news is mostly about the everyday basics of using AI at work. Research suggests the way leaders talk about AI shapes whether their people actually use it. Security and privacy keep coming up, from small-business cyber threats to a patched flaw in a popular chat app. The tools you may already use, like Google Workspace and Shopify, keep shifting under you, and a new wave of personal AI agents is arriving. Most of this week's other AI headlines were about big-company deals and models, and none of them changed much for a solo practice or small team.

OpenAI teams up with small business centers on AI training, and publishes a report on small-team use

OpenAI says it is partnering with America's SBDC (Small Business Development Centers) to offer hands-on AI training and local support to small businesses. It also released a report on how small teams use AI. The report comes from a company that sells AI tools, and the candidate text doesn't include its findings or methods, so read the numbers with that in mind. The training offer is the concrete part.

Why it matters: Free or low-cost local help with AI could lower the barrier for owners who don't know where to start, and the report may show what peers are actually doing.

Try this: Look up your local SBDC and ask whether it offers AI workshops. Skim the report for use cases that match your work, and keep in mind who wrote it.

Sources: openai.com

A flaw in ChatGPT's Mac app could have exposed sensitive data (now patched)

Wired reports that a recently patched vulnerability in ChatGPT's Mac app could have let hackers grab sensitive data. The story's point is that AI apps are now targets themselves, not just tools for attackers. The flaw has been fixed, and the summary doesn't say whether anyone was affected.

Why it matters: If you or your clients paste confidential session notes or business details into an AI app, that app's security becomes part of your duty to protect client privacy.

Try this: Make sure your AI apps are set to update automatically, and avoid pasting names or sensitive details you wouldn't want leaked.

Sources: wired.com

Shopify lets merchants build and edit an online store by chatting with its AI

Shopify has launched Canvas, a site builder where merchants describe changes to its AI agent, Sidekick, and watch their store update in real time. This is Shopify's own description, and we haven't seen independent testing. It's one more sign that website builders are moving from drag-and-drop to plain-language requests.

Why it matters: Owners who sell products, programs or digital downloads online may be able to make site changes without hiring a designer, though quality and control are still open questions.

Try this: If you use Shopify, try one small change, like rewording a product page, and check the result carefully before publishing.

Sources: techcrunch.com

Google is replacing Gems with 'skills' in Gemini and Workspace

Google says skills, which are reusable instructions that guide Gemini, are rolling out to Workspace users over the coming weeks. They will eventually replace Gems, the custom helpers some people built. Google's post includes dates for the transition away from Gems.

Why it matters: If your practice or team relies on a custom Gem, like a client-email drafter or a session-prep helper, it will need to move over.

Try this: List any Gems you use, then read Google's post for the transition dates so nothing disappears mid-project.

Sources: workspaceupdates.googleblog.com

OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse: personal AI agents arrive for everyday users

OpenAI announced Dots, a personal AI agent (an assistant that can take actions for you, not just chat), to compete with Meta's Muse. Both use friendly, cartoon-like characters. A Wired writer who tried both says he suspects readers will too, and Zapier has published a how-to for Muse. These are early reviews, not tested results, and we don't have independent data on reliability or price.

Why it matters: Your clients, and soon your customers, may start handing tasks to personal agents, and you may be tempted to do the same with email and calendars.

Try this: If you try one, start with a low-stakes task, like organizing a to-do list, and check what permissions it asks for.

Sources: wired.com · theverge.com · zapier.com

Worth watching

  • Meta disputes a journalist's claim that its Muse agent read his private messages while the required Mac setting was off, a reminder to check what permissions any agent really has. Source
  • A PwC survey finds business and tech leaders disagree on who is responsible for AI risk at work, a gap small teams can close by naming one person. Source
  • A federal judge dismissed antitrust lawsuits over Google's AI Overviews, so the traffic drop that AI search answers cause for websites is unlikely to be fixed in court soon. Source

One thing to explore: Zapier's roundup of the 7 best meeting scheduler apps

If you still trade emails to book sessions or client calls, a scheduling app can handle the back-and-forth, block open slots in your calendar and send the video link. Spend 20 minutes with Zapier's comparison, pick one that has a free tier, and test it with one friendly client. Zapier makes its own automation tools, so weigh its picks accordingly. Start here

item.title: Tuesday, September 29, 2026: Meta is bringing its Muse AI agent to small businesses
item.description: Much of this week's AI news is about "agents": assistants that act for you across your apps instead of just answering questions. Meta and OpenAI both pushed them toward everyday users, and one early mishap shows the privacy risks are real. For coaches, the more useful evidence this week is about what AI is doing to jobs, and it points in two directions. For small business owners, the practical questions are what to let an agent touch, and how to protect your AI accounts and your client data.
item.content:encoded:
Much of this week's AI news is about "agents": assistants that act for you across your apps instead of just answering questions. Meta and OpenAI both pushed them toward everyday users, and one early mishap shows the privacy risks are real. For coaches, the more useful evidence this week is about what AI is doing to jobs, and it points in two directions. For small business owners, the practical questions are what to let an agent touch, and how to protect your AI accounts and your client data.

Meta is bringing its Muse AI agent to small businesses

Meta is expanding Muse, its personal AI agent, to small business owners. Meta says it can help run a business and find new customers. Separately, Zapier says its connector is now available inside Muse. Once you authorize it, Muse can work across thousands of apps, but only the specific apps and actions you approve. The details of what Muse does for businesses come from Meta and Zapier, and we have no independent testing yet.

Why it matters: An always-on assistant tied to your customer messages and marketing could save a solo owner real time, but it also gets access to sensitive information.

Try this: If you try it, start with read-only access and one low-stakes task, and don't connect anything that holds client notes or payment details.

Sources: techcrunch.com · zapier.com

Meta's Muse agent reportedly gave out a user's home address to a stranger

Tech YouTuber Matt Robb says Muse shared his home address with a stranger after he let it manage his Facebook Marketplace account. He says it also agreed to a lowball price, and the buyer showed up in person. The bot didn't tell him until late that night. This is one person's account, as reported by The Verge. It happened even though Meta stressed Muse's security features at launch.

Why it matters: If an agent can mishandle personal details in one marketplace chat, it can mishandle client or customer details in yours.

Try this: Before letting any AI agent talk to customers or clients for you, ask what personal information it can see, and whether you can review its messages before they go out.

Sources: theverge.com

OpenAI launches Dots, an always-on AI helper that works across your apps

OpenAI announced Dots, assistants that keep working in the background across connected apps and learn your preferences over time. The company says they can "do nearly anything" across more than 4,000 supported apps, using their own cloud computer and web browser. They start with paid ChatGPT Pro, Business Premium and Enterprise subscribers. Those abilities are OpenAI's own claims.

Why it matters: This is the same kind of hands-off assistant Meta is pushing, so owners will soon be choosing which one, if any, to trust with real work.

Try this: If you're on one of the eligible plans, test a Dot on something harmless, like organizing a public research folder, before connecting email or client files.

Sources: openai.com · theverge.com · wired.com

ChatGPT adds documents, slides and team workspaces, edging into office-suite territory

OpenAI added features that let teams create documents and presentations and work with AI agents inside ChatGPT. Coverage describes the new tools as Space, Pages and slides. TechCrunch says it puts OpenAI in more direct competition with traditional software companies like Microsoft, and ZDNET asks whether it could replace Google Workspace. It's early, and nothing in the coverage suggests it matches those tools yet.

Why it matters: If your AI tool is also where your documents live, it changes both your software costs and where client information is stored.

Try this: Try one non-confidential document in ChatGPT's new tools, and note where the file is stored and who on your team can see it.

Sources: zdnet.com · techcrunch.com

New study finds no sign yet that AI is cutting hiring of recent graduates

A working paper from researchers Robert Fairlie and Jane Wu at Munich's CESifo says there is "no evidence of any significant, widespread displacement or reduction in hiring of recent college graduates." It contradicts a Stanford study reported last month, which found entry-level employment in AI-exposed jobs lagging other fields. A working paper hasn't been through formal peer review. The two studies use different approaches, so the question is still open.

Why it matters: Many coaching clients, and their kids, are anxious about AI and early-career jobs, and the evidence doesn't yet support a simple story either way.

Try this: When a client raises AI job fears, ask what they've actually seen in their own field before offering reassurance or alarm.

Sources: arstechnica.com

When clients use AI to do work they once hired out

MIT Sloan Management Review describes a real estate firm whose in-house lawyers now use generative AI for lease work that outside counsel used to handle. The firm says it saves hundreds of thousands of dollars and cut delays from weeks. The outside law firms lost that work. The article looks at how service providers can respond, though we only have the opening of it here.

Why it matters: Any coach or consultant sells expertise that clients may increasingly try to replicate with AI, so it pays to know what you offer that they can't.

Try this: List the parts of your service a client could now do with a chatbot, and the parts that depend on your judgment, accountability or relationship.

Sources: sloanreview.mit.edu

Stolen AI logins are being sold, and businesses are paying the bills

ZDNET reports that Google analysts warn stolen AI account credentials are being sold underground. Attackers use them to run up usage, and the business that owns the account gets the bill. The practice is called "LLMjacking." The coverage focuses on businesses and how to stop it.

Why it matters: If you pay for AI tools or connect them to your systems, a leaked login can turn into a surprise charge or expose your data.

Try this: Check the billing page on each AI tool you use, set a spending limit if one is offered, and turn on two-step sign-in.

Sources: zdnet.com

Worth watching

  • MIT Technology Review asks who is legally responsible when an AI agent causes harm, a question that will matter to any business letting agents act on its behalf. Source
  • Microsoft is rolling out a new all-in-one Copilot app with agents, and ZDNET notes the pricing is still "evolving," so watch your Microsoft 365 bill. Source
  • McKinsey's new research on skills and pathways between shrinking and growing US occupations may help coaches working with clients in career transition. Source
